She has worn many hats as a businesswoman, mother, wife, widow, TV personality, author, radio host, and DJ. events.title: Giving Back on GivingTuesday! Join Us for a Healthy Forests Day of Action
events.description: This GivingTuesday, roll up your sleeves and help keep our local forests healthy! Scenic Rivers is teaming up with the Chesapeake Bay Foundation and Save our Trees (a program of Anne Arundel County Watershed Stewards Academy) for a special Healthy Forests volunteer workday removing invasive English ivy from trees at the Philip Merrill Environmental Center in Annapolis. The Chesapeake Bay Foundation’s beautiful waterfront campus is protected by a Scenic Rivers & MET conservation easement, and we’re excited to work together to care for this special place! Our GivingTuesday volunteers braved cold, rainy weather last year and still got an incredible amount of work done. We’re hoping for a little more sunshine this year, and we’ll celebrate a job well done with pizza on the deck overlooking the Bay! As part of Scenic Rivers Healthy Forests program, volunteers will work in designated areas of the conservation easement to remove English ivy from trees. Invasive vines can damage and weaken trees. Removing harmful invasive vines is an important step toward protecting the health of our local forests. No experience necessary! We’ll provide training on how to identify and safely remove English ivy. Scenic Rivers and Save Our Trees will provide work gloves and tools, though volunteers are welcome to bring their own. What to Wear and Bring: Wear long sleeves, long pants, and closed-toe shoes. Poison ivy is present in the work areas. Bring a full water bottle. Dress for the weather! We’ll be working outdoors in early December. Keeping our forests healthy takes teamwork! GivingTuesday is the perfect opportunity to make a difference right here in our community. We hope you’ll join us! Questions? Contact Scenic Rivers Stewardship and Engagement Coordinator, Luke Lanham, at Luke@srlt.org or 443.714.7756.

events.title: Kate Voegele "Then & Now" Tour
events.description: Singer-songwriter and One Tree Hill alum Kate Voegele returns to the stage with Then & Now, an intimate new tour built around the songs — and the stories behind them. After revisiting the music of One Tree Hill on tour last year, Voegele is digging deeper into the catalog this time, bringing back songs from her years as Mia Catalano that haven’t been heard live in years alongside music from her new album, Age of Alchemy. Built around storytelling and songwriting, Then & Now traces the unexpected threads between songs Voegele wrote at the beginning of her career and the artist she is today — how the same emotions change with time, what she understands differently now, and the stories behind the songs that she’s never shared before. Part concert, part trip through the pages of her songwriting history, Then & Now offers fans a rare chance to experience nearly two decades of Kate Voegele’s music in a completely new way: the old songs, the new songs, and everything that happened in between. events.title: Roundtable: Diasporas as Strategic Actors
events.description: Diasporas represent influential actors at the intersection of international affairs, economic development, entrepreneurship, migration, and geopolitics. Beyond remittances and cultural ties, diaspora communities shape international business, trade, innovation ecosystems, investment flows, talent circulation, institutional development, and transnational engagement strategies. However, growing geopolitical fragmentation and poly-globalization, conflict-driven displacement, rising nationalism, digital connectivity and AI are transforming how diasporas and sending and receiving countries interact. This suggests that prior ways of operating in and as diasporas face various challenges and disruptions calling for adaptations and resilient approaches. Existing scholarship highlights both the political and economic dimensions of diaspora engagement. Harris Mylonas has examined diaspora politics, state-diaspora relations, and nationalism while investigating how states cultivate, manage, and mobilize diasporic populations. Jennifer Brinkerhoff has demonstrated how diasporas contribute to development, institutional reform, and public-private collaboration. Maria Elo has built on their work advancing understanding of diaspora entrepreneurship, migrant and refugee business activity, transnational networks, and talent mobility. Together, these perspectives developed at GWU and its diaspora program provide a unique setting for understanding diasporas as strategic actors in a changing world.

Twelve years after their founding, The War And Treaty have redefined themselves beyond Academy of Country Music, Country Music Association, and GRAMMY nominations. events.title: What Do We Mean By PrEP (Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis)?
events.description: What Do We Mean By PrEP? Featuring Dr. Maranda Ward, '17, Associate Professor and Director of Equity, Department of Clinical Research & Leadership, GW School of Medicine and Health Sciences PrEP, or Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis, is a safe and highly effective medication that helps prevent HIV infection. Yet many people and communities who could benefit from PrEP are not using it. Why? In this talk, Dr. Maranda Ward will explore how public health messaging, research, and healthcare practices shape people's understanding of PrEP and influence who feels seen, supported, and informed when making decisions about HIV prevention. Drawing on her research, Dr. Ward will discuss the importance of moving beyond stigma and deficit-based narratives toward approaches that recognize the strengths, experiences, and realities of diverse communities. The talk will explore PrEP's role in HIV prevention, the structural inequities that continue to affect access and uptake, and why equitable, intersectional communication and education is essential to reaching and resonating with those who stand to benefit most. About Dr. Maranda Ward: Dr. Maranda C. Ward is an Associate Professor in the Department of Clinic

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: History Talk: Hardtack and Hard Times: Civil War Food and the U.S. Army
events.venue: National Museum of the United States Army
events.description: Healthy Soldiers are essential for the U.S. Army to accomplish its mission. The food Soldiers eat is one way to keep a strong fighting force. The vitamins and minerals that make up a Soldier’s diet ensure that they are capable of enduring the physical and mental requirements to be successful. Since the Revolutionary War, the U.S. Army has experimented with and provided food to Soldiers based on available resources, nutrition, and current technology. Coffee, hardtack, and salt pork comprised the majority of a Civil War Soldier’s diet. While these items may seem crude by 21st century standards, they met the nutritional needs of Soldiers at the time. The U.S. Army ration—the amount of food authorized for one Soldier per day—kept Soldiers’ stomachs full and gave them the energy to move forward. In this History Talk, explore how the U.S. Army supplied its Soldiers during the Civil War. Learn how Soldiers supplemented their rations and, for many, learned to cook for the first time. As part of the field trip, you’ll also learn how to cook like a Civil War Soldier and make hardtack at home. Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: Mike Tramp of White Lion (Solo Acoustic)
events.description: Mike Tramp, legendary White Lion singer, songwriter and front man stepped out on his own in 1995 and began his 29-year long solo career. With twelve consistent solo albums to his name, you can easily say that he has stood his ground. Tramp has never steered off his path and is charging forward with confidence, and no desire to look back. Tramp says, "It really just meant that I knew who I wanted to be and sound like when I recorded my first solo album twenty-five years ago. Yet, one thing led to another, and as they say, you shouldn't let sleeping lions sleep for too long." Therefore, after much request to bring the White Lion songs back to the live circuit, Mike Tramp re-recorded 12 of White Lion's greatest hits, and also gave it a natural facelift, since it had been close to 40 years since the songs were originally written and recorded. The album, titled "Mike Tramp - Songs of White Lion" was released in April 2023 to rave reviews, with many saying how fresh and today the songs sounded. Some even said it sounded like a brand new album. The album brought Mike Tramp's White Lion around the world and included two tours of the USA in 2023. One thing led to another, and this August, "Songs Of White Lion Vol. II" will hit the streets followed by a two month tour across the USA with Mike Tramp's White Lion. Tramp says "White Lion was a chapter and a journey I was on; it was a one-way ticket with no return. The hair trend of the decade has since faded, but the music lives on, stronger than ever. He states, "It's both challenging and a joy for me. Still, the truth is that people don't know that most of these big rock songs started out as folk songs in a Brooklyn, NY basement."Which is the true secret to why they still work on stage. You can't keepа good song down.

events.title: Pivot to Asia 3.0? Navigating Future Alliances in Northeast Asia
events.description: This talk explores a “Pivot 3.0” under new domestic political and geopolitical circumstances in the U.S. and in Northeast Asia. The United States first pivoted toward the Indo-Pacific under the Obama administration, and subsequent administrations have continued, rebranded, or reshaped that orientation. Meanwhile, Northeast Asia’s strategic environment has shifted dramatically, driven by China’s growing assertiveness, North Korea’s expanding nuclear capabilities and diplomatic ties with China and Russia, and competing demands on U.S. attention and resources. This talk explores a “Pivot 3.0” under new domestic political and geopolitical circumstances in the U.S. and in the region. It examines how allies and partners are recalibrating and which contemporary tensions are testing traditional alliances. The talk concludes with what a “Pivot 3.0” could look like as regional and U.S. stakeholders chart new engagements. Doors will open no sooner than 15 minutes before the start time. events.title: Symposia on Government Oversight and Accountability: Civil Society and the Fourth Estate
events.description: This December, the Symposium on Government Oversight and Accountability turns to oversight beyond government itself. Panelists will examine how civil society organizations and investigative journalists hold public institutions accountable, how they engage with all three branches of government, and what recent developments suggest about the future of oversight. Jay N. Lerner, lecturer at the Trachtenberg School, will host a discussion with panelists James-Christian Blockwood, president and CEO of the National Academy of Public Administration; Jessie Durrett, director of public policy and stakeholder engagement at the Partnership for Public Service; Jesse Eisinger, assistant managing editor at ProPublica; and Daniel Weiner, senior director at the Brennan Center for Justice. The hybrid event will take place on December 2 at noon. Location and registration link coming soon!

events.title: The Grit and the Grind: Book Talk Featuring Dr. Joshua L. Glazer
events.description: The Grit and the Grind: Building High-Performing Education Systems in an Era of Polarization Book Talk featuring Dr. Joshua L. Glazer, Author and GW Professor of Education Policy Moderated by Dr. Matthew Shirrell, Associate Professor of Educational Leadership and Administration While school improvement depends in part on choosing strong curricula, recruiting talented leaders, and adopting effective organizational models, it also requires organizations to learn from experience, build professional capacity, and gradually develop coherent systems for teaching and learning. This work unfolds within political, historical, and social contexts that can either provide or undermine the trust, stability, and time that organizational learning and sustained improvement require. The Grit and the Grind argues that politics, history, and system improvement are therefore inseparable. Political conditions shape whether reforms acquire legitimacy, while legitimacy, in turn, influences whether organizations have the opportunity to acknowledge mistakes, revise strategies, build professional knowledge, and develop increasingly effective instructional systems. Drawing on nearly a decade of research in Memphis, the authors develop this argument through a comparison of two ambitious efforts to transform some of Tennessee's lowest-performing schools: the state-run Achievement School District (ASD) and Shelby County Schools' Innovation Zone (iZone). events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. Image: Once Known Mende carver [Mende, Sierra Leone], Sowei, 19th-20th century, wood, varnish, 16 H x 10 W x 10 D in. Gift of Stephen A. Spear, 1975 (P.75.2.30)

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. Regina has appeared with folk pioneer Tret Fure and feminist icon Ani DiFranco, and her former duo Porter & Sayles was featured on the Melissa Etheridge Cruise. Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Les Misérables-Olney Theatre
events.description: Modern classics don’t come any bigger than Les Misérables, and Olney Theatre celebrates it for the first time in honor of the show’s 40th anniversary. Based on Victor Hugo’s sweeping 19th-century novel of redemption, revolution, and love, the songs of Les Miz conquered Broadway in the 1980s and continue to resonate in this third decade of the 21st Century. Follow Jean-Valjean from his beginnings as convict #24601 to life in hiding, to protector of Cosette, pursued all the while by the relentless Javert, culminating in the revolutionary passions of the 1832 Paris uprising. Join us at the barricade this holiday season, and be stirred by a musical unmatched by its lyrical humor, its calls for justice, and its portrayal of the sacrifices one can make in the name of love. Featuring: Kevin S. McAllister as Javert, Alex De Bard as Eponine, Tracy Lynn Olivera as Madame Thénardier, Jordan Friend as Thénardier, Stephanie Waters as Fantine, Ben Clark as Marius, and more to be announced soon.

events.title: Mental Reset: Sound Bath + Reiki : Thursday Evenings in Falls Church
events.address: 7777 Leesburg Pike, Ste 204S, Falls Church, VA 22043
events.description: Thursday is a weird day. The week isn't over, but you are. Mental Reset is one hour at the end of the workday where nobody needs anything from you. You come in, you lie down on a mat, you get a blanket and a bolster, and for the next sixty minutes your only job is to listen. I play crystal singing bowls, guide you through a short meditation so your mind has something to do besides replay the day, and offer Reiki while you rest. Most people tell me some version of the same thing afterward: the noise in their head finally turned down. Not off: down. Enough that they can go home and actually be home, instead of answering emails in their head at the dinner table. You don't need experience. You don't need to know how to meditate, and you definitely don't need to “clear your mind.” If you could do that, you wouldn't need this class. First-timers are in the room most weeks. There are ten spots. That's deliberate. It's a small room, I can see everyone in it, and it never feels like an event. It feels like an exhale. A few regulars started as skeptics; more than one of our Google reviews comes from someone who arrived doubting the whole thing and left surprised at how settled they felt. You don't have to believe in anything for an hour of sound and rest to do you some good. Run by Victoria Vita: CPA for 20+ years, healer for 7+. I sat behind a desk with a brain that wouldn't switch off for a long time before I found this work. Thursday nights are built for the person I used to be. Rated 5.0 from 32 Google reviews. Come straight from work. Leave like the week let go of you first. What's included: • 60 minutes of crystal singing bowls, guided meditation and Reiki • Mat, blanket, and bolster everything is here; you bring nothing • Small group: 10 people maximum, same teacher every week • Time at the end to sit up slowly, have water, and not rush out Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.description: Nature Thursdays invites preschool-aged explorers to join Gunston Educators for themed storytimes and nature hikes through the woods and waterways on the grounds of Gunston Hall in Fairfax County, Virginia. Running on the first Thursday of every month at 10:30 a.m., this program helps young ecologists gain essential skills including preschool readiness, respect for the environment, gross and fine motor refinement, and self-expression. Each month features a different theme, from Preparedness in February to Winter in December, creating year-round opportunities for children to connect with nature and outdoor learning. Exploratory activities encourage curiosity and environmental stewardship while building confidence in young learners. The program runs rain or shine, so families are encouraged to practice outdoor preparedness and dress for the weather. An adult must accompany all children. Nature Thursdays offers an engaging, hands-on approach to early childhood education set in Gunston Hall's natural setting. Discover More Attractions in #FXVA

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

REIMAGINING THE CANON: African Art, Display, and Interpretation
events.description: This is a public-facing lecture and reception to accompany the exhibition "Unfossilizing African Art" on view now at the Brady Gallery. Read more about the exhibition: Unfossilizing African Art - Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication.

events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.title: The Darkened Light of Faith
events.description: Could the African American political tradition save American democracy? African Americans have had every reason to reject America’s democratic experiment. Yet African American activists, intellectuals, and artists who have sought to transform the United States into a racially just society have put forward some of the most original and powerful ideas about how to make America live up to its democratic ideals. In The Darkened Light of Faith, Melvin Rogers provides a bold new account of African American political thought through the works and lives of individuals who built this vital tradition—a tradition that is urgently needed today. The book reexamines how figures as diverse as David Walker, Frederick Douglass, Anna Julia Cooper, Ida B. Wells, W.E.B. Du Bois, Billie Holiday, and James Baldwin thought about the politics, people, character, and culture of a society that so often dominated them. Sharing a light of faith darkened but not extinguished by the tragic legacy of slavery, they resisted the conclusion that America would always be committed to white supremacy. They believed that democracy is always in the process of becoming and that they could use it to reimagine society. But they also saw that achieving racial justice wouldn’t absolve us of the darkest features of our shared past, and that democracy must be measured by how skillfully we confront a history that will forever remain with us. events.description: Join Professor Laura Katzman as she discusses the public art of Ben Shahn (1898-1969), focusing on his most prominent New Deal fresco murals, The Meaning of Social Security, which were commissioned by the Public Works Agency’s Section of Fine Arts (1940-1942) for the Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building in Washington, DC. Dr. Katzman will address how Shahn navigated the demands of federal agencies, the needs of his own art and activism, and the larger goals of his social criticism. The program will illuminate the status of Shahn’s murals in the context of the current administration’s controversial efforts to sell specific government buildings and its drastic staff cuts to the General Services Administration—the official steward of federally funded art in government buildings across the United States. Katzman’s lecture will be accompanied by a conversation with former director of the U.S. General Services Administration’s Center for Fine Arts, Jennifer Gibson. Presented in partnership with Moment Magazine. ABOUT THE SPEAKERS Laura Katzman is a professor of art history at James Madison University, and has served as the Terra Foundation Professor of American Art at the Free University Berlin. An internationally recognized scholar of documentary photography in the United States and Puerto Rico, Dr. Katzman has co-authored numerous publications, including Ben Shahn’s New York: The Photography of Modern Times (2000), Re-viewing Documentary: The Photographic Life of Louise Rosskam (2014), and The Museum of the Old Colony: An Art Installation by Pablo Delano (2023). Her most recent book, Ben Shahn, On Nonconformity (2025), accompanied the eponymous and highly acclaimed retrospective that she curated for the Museo Reina Sofia in Madrid (2023-2024) and adapted for the Jewish Museum in New York (2025). events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. We do this all—in small and grand gestures, every day— in service of learning with and for each other in the crafting of the world we wish to see. Perhaps we are ar

events.description: Take a student-led tour of the exhibitions currently on view at the Brady Art Gallery: "Unfossilizing African Art" and "Cracks and Reforms". events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cooking in the Archives: Circulating Recipes & 17th-century Ice Cream
events.description: Prof. Marissa Nicosia shares her research on Elisabeth Hawar’s 1687 recipe book, which includes a tantalizing, early English recipe for ice cream. Recipe books are important texts for researching the history of Renaissance food and medicine, the expanding global trade in culinary ingredients, the practices of cooking and preservation labor in the household, and the circulation of knowledge. Nicosia’s research unfolds in the kitchen as well as in the library as she seeks to learn about flavors and cookery methods from the past that we might experience anew today. Professor Marissa Nicosia is a Professor of Renaissance Literature in the English Program at Penn State Abington, where she teaches, researches and writes about early modern English literature, food studies, book history, and political theory. Her public food history website, Cooking in the Archives features more than a hundred updated recipes and has had approximately 340,000 visitors. This event is generously sponsored by GWU English and is free and open to the public.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. Gift from the Trustees of the Corcoran Gallery of Art (Gift of Gail & Robert Carlsen in memory of Tom Ryan) (CGA.2004.26.01) © Boris Ignatovich

events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.title: Fabric Fundamentals Part 2: Tools, Techniques, and Care
events.description: This class dives into the practical side of fabric handling, giving you the knowledge and tools to approach various textiles with confidence. We will start at the cutting table and go to the finished project: knowing how different fabrics respond to different cutting tools and techniques, choosing the right needles and thread for your fabric, understanding how your sewing machine’s settings will affect the fabric (or even which machine you use!), and selecting the presser feet that will make your work easier and cleaner. We’ll also cover pressing settings that protect delicate fibers while getting the job done. Finally, we will take the mystery out of care labels and learn to decode what they actually mean and how to wash, dry, and care for specific fiber types so whether it is your creation or off the rack, your garments can look great for years to come. This class is designed to provide a daytime introductory course option to the community. It is perfect for anyone looking to increase their ability to navigate and handle the fabrics they sew, anyone curious about sewing, homeschool students looking for outside instruction, or for those who have not sewn in years and would benefit from a guided refresher. This fabric course is designed to complement other Sew It Begins classes. Look for Fabric Fundamentals 1: Identifying Textile Attributes.

We also will discuss some of the fabled residents of the two mansions the organization now occupies, including the former homes of President James Monroe and his First Lady Elizabeth, and Civil War General Robert MacFeely. events.title: Gallery B Presents “Cathedral of Silence: Layers of Time and Coexistence” by Kee Woo Rhee
events.description: Kee Woo Rhee’s photographic journey is a sacred pilgrimage into the deepest, unviolated sanctuaries of the earth—the primeval forests. This exhibition brings together a rigorous visual anthology of the world’s most venerable temperate rainforests: the ancient giants of MacMillan Provincial Park in Vancouver, Canada, the moss-draped silence of the Hoh Rain Forest in the United States, and the pristine, untold woodland cathedrals of Croatia. Through her lens, these distinct geographical landscapes converge into a single, transcendent spiritual topography. “Standing amidst the colossal architecture of these ancient woods, I do not merely observe nature; I encounter the Cathedral of Silence.” Gallery hours are Wednesday – Saturdays, 11am – 6pm; Sundays, 12 – 5pm. There will be an opening reception Saturday, December 5 from 4 – 7pm. The gallery will be closed December 24 – 25 and January 1.

events.description: Liz Longley is a Nashville-based singer-songwriter whose candid lyrics move through Americana, pop-rock, gospel-tinged soul and jazz. A Berklee College of Music graduate and BMI John Lennon Songwriting Scholarship Competition honoree, she turns intimate stories into songs that feel both personal and widely recognizable. Her album Funeral For My Past—funded independently with more than $150,000 raised by fans—includes “Send You My Love” and “Finally High”; earlier releases include Weightless and the self-titled Liz Longley. Longley’s expressive vocals and genre-spanning melodies give her songwriting room to shift from reflective to richly energized.

events.title: Liz Longley with Special Guests The Young Fables: The Holiday Fuss Tour
events.description: Nashville-based singer-songwriter Liz Longley embarks on her very first Christmas tour, supporting her forthcoming EP The Holiday Fuss, a collection of original songs capturing the warmth, chaos, and magic of the season. Known for her stop-you-in-your-tracks voice and deeply personal songwriting, Longley has built a devoted following through albums like Funeral For My Past and New Life, establishing herself as one of Americana and folk's most beloved voices. Her 2020 debut Christmas EP A Little Magic introduced her festive side, and this second holiday collection deepens her love for the season and the stories it inspires. For longtime fans, this is a rare and intimate opportunity to experience Longley in a completely different light—festive, joyful, and full of the same emotional depth that defines her artistry. Expect the kind of genuine warmth and vulnerability that makes her live performances unforgettable, all wrapped in holiday spirit. Jammin' Java welcomes this cherished artist to Fairfax County, Virginia.

events.title: Lukas Nelson Live: A Special Solo Acoustic Performance of Songs & Stories (Matinee)
events.description: GRAMMY and BAFTA Award-winning singer, songwriter and musician Lukas Nelson has established himself as one of music’s most respected voices. Throughout his esteemed career, Nelson has released eight studio albums including his latest, 2023's Sticks and Stones. Since its release, the album spent 18 weeks in the top 10 of the Americana Albums chart and earned Nelson two #1 singles: "Sticks and Stones," which reached #1 on the Alt Country chart and "More Than Friends," feat. Lainey Wilson, which topped the Americana Singles chart. Additionally, "More Than Friends" is also nominated for Collaborative Video of the Year at the 2024 CMT Music Awards. Released to widespread critical acclaim, The Wall Street Journal praises, “[Nelson] makes the genre his own...This is a fresh and welcome addition to what he’s offered so far,” while The Tennessean declared, “thoughtful, timeless Southern-style rock featuring anything from introspective lyricism to virtuoso-style musicianship.” Since his debut over a decade ago, the Texas and Hawaii-based artist has performed countless sold-out headline dates and festivals, demonstrating the electric energy of his live shows. events.title: Research & Enrichment! Science with Your Dog
events.description: Join the GW Dog Lab for fun, free enrichment with your dog! The GW Canine Cognition Collaborative (aka GW Dog Lab) is a student-run lab in the Anthropology Department. Research sessions are on campus, after hours and on weekends, and are designed to last only 1 hour. Because humans and dogs share an environment, we can learn a lot about the way that environment has shaped our species by comparing dog and toddler cognition. We play simple games with dogs designed to measure their cognition and then compare them to toddlers. How to Participate 1. Start by submitting a pre-screening form. This helps us learn about your dog 2. Next, open your email and look for your onboarding information sent from canine.cognition@gwu.edu. 3. Then, using the information in your email, sign up for your initial visit. This is a get-to-know-you visit that makes it easier for dogs to get acclimated to our testing space. 4. Finally, after the initial visit, depending on your dog's comfort level, you will get email invitations to studies your dog is eligible for! Parking information can be found on the GW Dog Lab website.

events.description: Professor of Violin James Stern and Audrey Andrist, piano, take to the stage with UMWO for a performance of Berg’s Concerto for Violin, Piano and 13 Wind Instruments. Fri Dec 04 8:00pm To – 10:00pm The Clarice Smith Performing Arts Center Buy Tickets Clarice website Add to Calendar Alban Berg composed his Concerto for Violin, Piano and 13 Wind Instruments as a belated 50th-birthday gift for his mentor, Arnold Schoenberg. Inscribed at the top were the words “Aller Guten Dinge sind Drei,” or, “All good things come in threes.” This refers to a number of compositional decisions, including the number of movements and the number of performing units, but also to the trio of friends whose names are used to create the theme of the first movement: Schoenberg, Webern and Berg. At its essence, Berg’s composition is testament to friendship, and is rich with musical and programmatic meaning that reflects the compositional world of 1920s Vienna. events.title: Triangle Art Studios Presents “Luminance: Contained” by Susan Darrow
events.description: “Luminance Contained ” will feature black & white works by Rockville-based fine art photographer Susan Darrow. Darrow first picked up a camera in high school, learning old-school techniques of darkroom developing and printing. She uses a full-format digital camera with a large sensor to capture maximum sharp detail, and carefully composes the best possible photograph in-camera, minimizing post-production editing. Darrow is drawn to Black & White Photography because of the stability and order it brings to what was once a chaotic scene. “The tones are all connected to each other, and what was once a jostling combustion of color at once becomes peaceful.” The exhibition runs November 20 through December 27. Gallery hours are Fridays & Saturdays, 10am – 5pm; Sundays, 11am – 2pm. There will be an opening reception Saturday, November 21, 5 – 8pm. The exhibit will also be open for the Bethesda Art Walk on Friday, December 11, 6 – 8pm.

events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. events.title: Working Session: Strengthening Support for Open Source and Research Infrastructure
events.description: Following the two-day Summit on Open-Source Ecosystems (SOSE) Summit at George Mason, this smaller workshop brings together leaders of the organizations that help open source ecosystems function: enabling organizations like university OSPOs, research libraries, fiscal sponsors, and funders, and ecosystem amplifiers like open source foundations, community organizations, and field-building alliances. Each offers a different kind of support, but these organizations rarely have opportunities to connect their capabilities or coordinate their work, a gap that matters more as disruptions to research funding create new pressures across the ecosystem. Over the evening and day together, our central question will be how enabling organizations and ecosystem amplifiers can better connect their knowledge and resources to strengthen support for open source and research infrastructure. This event is by invitation only.

events.title: A Gift in Motion
events.description: A multidisciplinary showcase from the artists and scholars of the full-time faculty and staff at the Corcoran School of the Arts & Design. A Gift In Motion loosely draws from Robin Wall Kimmerer’s book The Serviceberry which uplifts Indigenous frameworks of the natural world to advance the possibilities in collectivity, reciprocity, and the mindset of abundance. These are anti-capitalist models and theories that provide insight into the systems of power we negotiate, but also offer a lens on how we individually move through our daily lives—together—through historically fraught landscapes. A keen reminder that working with, for, and because of each other remains the most human motivation, even while we are inundated with narratives that suggest otherwise. Within the walls of the academy, frameworks of artistic and creative knowledge are often dismissed, as are Indigenous methodologies and community-focused perspectives that center human engagement, oral and craft-based practices, and unquantifiable research. A personal experience. A feeling. Abstraction. And yet, for centuries, within the walls of art schools exist myriad economies of imagination that are anchored in the sharing of diverse creative knowledge and articulated in what we make, write, perform, dance, build, conserve, collect, display, speak, and think. events.description: Take a student-led tour of the exhibitions currently on view at the Brady Art Gallery: "Unfossilizing African Art" and "Cracks and Reforms". Unfossilizing African Art recontextualizes African material culture objects that have been held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students across four seminar courses conducted original research to deepen understanding of the collection and reconsider how these objects are interpreted and exhibited. Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection examines a decade shaped by political upheaval, social transformation, migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition. This exhibition, developed as part of an art history class taught by Associate Professor Bibi Obler, is accompanied by a catalog designed by graphic design students.

events.title: Cannupa Hanska Luger’s REFLECT
events.description: REFLECT traces the evolution of artist Cannuap Hanska Luger’s Mirror Shield Project. In 2016, when the Dakota Access Pipeline threatened the waters of his ancestral homelands, Luger circulated a video demonstrating how to make “mirror shields” from inexpensive materials. Conceived during the Indigenous-led resistance at Standing Rock, North Dakota, the tutorial functioned as a call to collective action, an invitation for people across the country to stand in solidarity with the Water Protectors. Carried by Water Protectors in frontline actions and collective formations, the mirrored surfaces offered protection while redirecting the field of vision. More than a thousand mirror shields were created and transported to the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ camp. The exhibition brings the project’s history into the present, treating the archive as a resource to be carried forward and put into practice. Photographs, videos, garments, ephemera, and community-generated documentation reveal a collective artwork shaped by those who made, carried, adapted, interpreted, and activated it.

events.title: Cracks & Reforms: The 1920s Through the GW Collection
events.description: The 1920s emerged as a decade suspended between collapse and reconstruction, an era marked by “cracks and reforms” that ushered in a profound reconfiguration of the visual world. During this period marked by civil transformation and political upheaval, artists, journalists, and makers had opportunities to reconstruct both individual and collective identities. A century later, Cracks & Reforms presents a distinct cross-section of this period, revealing global currents of migration, modernization, and cultural redefinition through the lens of the GW Collection. Students led by Associate Professor Bibiana Obler selected works to study and exhibit, their research eventually leading to unified themes and a catalog designed by Corcoran graphic design students led by professors Sharmila Karamchandani and Aasawari Kulkarni. Image: Boris Ignatovich (Russian, 1899-1976), Composer Dmitri Shostakovich, from "Ignatovich, Soviet Avant-Garde", 1928, gelatin silver print, 16 H x 20 W in. events.title: Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY
events.description: For Freedoms presents artist and educator Eric Gottesman’s NIGHT AND DAY which centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1984 Amharic novel Oromay, written under the Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on Gottesman’s deep engagement with the novel, NIGHT AND DAY considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence. The exhibition extends beyond the gallery through a library of banned books, a self-guided workshop station that invites visitors to respond to censorship through writing and drawing, and a public conversation on how artists sustain creative practice amid sociopolitical pressure.

events.description: Exhibition Openings: Solo Artists, Clustered Spires Quilt Guild & Baltimore Watercolor Society Saturday, December 5 • 3–5 pm FREE View exhibitions and meet the artists! These exhibitions are opening on Saturday, December 5 and can be viewed starting at 9 am. Beat the crowds and visit us earlier in the day! Dec 5–27 Clustered Spires Quilt Guild It’s A Quilted Life Fiber This exhibition features members of the Clustered Spires Quilt Guild who have made work from two themed challenges: create a quilt that illustrates your favorite song and one that uses geometric shapes as a point of departure. Dec 5–27 Cynthia Baush & Rennie Blalock Reconciliation Photo collage and soft pastel The work in this exhibition is a reflection of hope for reconciliation of the cultural divides affecting us in politics, class, religion, gender, and culture and the boundaries put in place between humanity and the natural world. Dec 5–27 Johan Lowie Silent Witness Mixed media This series of intimate portraits were created on the pages of discarded books using pencil, watercolor, and acrylic. They focus on fleeting expressions, gestures, and moments of recognition. Their modest scale invites close looking, encouraging viewers to slow down and engage with the humanity found in ordinary, often overlooked moments. Dec 5–January 31 Baltimore Watercolor Society Small Works by Signature Members of the Baltimore Watercolor Society Watercolor With a wide range of subject matter and techniques, the work in this exhibition comes from Signature Members of The Baltimore Watercolor Society, one of America’s oldest watercolor societies. This exhibit will include awards for 1st, 2nd, 3rd and Honorable Mentions by BWS selected juror, Luis Perez.

events.title: Fall Birding Series E: Patuxent Research Refuge, South Tract, MD
events.address: 8940 Jones Mill Road, Chevy Chase, MD 20815
events.description: Leaders: Rob Hilton and Lisa Shannon Members $33; nonmembers $46 Our fall birding series visit natural areas under an hour’s drive from DC where a variety of habitats – including field, forest, and wetland – provide good opportunities for the observation and ID of birds in autumn. On the earliest walks, we’ll hope to catch some southbound migrants – including those “confusing fall warblers.” As the season progresses, we’ll watch for sparrows, raptors, waterfowl, and other birds, both resident and overwintering in the region. These teaching walks are aimed at beginning to mid-level birders, but all are welcome. Our explorations will be on mostly level, natural surface trails that may be uneven, muddy, and/or somewhat slippery. REGISTER.

events.title: Fort Tour
events.address: 13551 Fort Washington Road, Fort Washington, MD 20744
events.description: Are you curious about the fascinating history behind Fort Washington? Join us for an enlightening guided tour that delves into the who, what, where, when, and why of this historic fortification! Discover the strategic significance of Digges Point and uncover the reasons it was selected as the ideal site for building the fort. Whether you are a history buff or just looking to enjoy a scenic walk through the fort, this tour is perfect for all ages. Our knowledgeable guides will provide insights into the fort’s construction, its role in defense, and the stories of those who lived and served here. In the event of incliment weather (dangerous heat, thunderstorms, poor air quality, or freezing cold) this program will be moved inside the visitor center and abridge to 30 minutes. If you’re interested in participating but the scheduled times don’t work for you, please don’t hesitate to reach out! Call the Visitor Center at 771-208-1555 or email us prior to your arrival, and we’ll do our best to accommodate your request for a different tour time.

events.description: Who led the Civil Rights protests to desegregate Glen Echo Amusement Park in 1960? Which amusement park ride was a focal point of the protests? events.title: GLEN ECHO POTTERY
events.description: Visit the Glen Echo Pottery Gallery to view ceramic work by instructors and advanced students. Open Saturdays & Sundays, 11am - 4pm, April - December. Glen Echo Pottery was founded by Jeff Kirk, who has been the Artistic Director, full-time artist-in-residence, and chief instructor since 1974. He managed the Pottery as a sole proprietorship until 2003, when it was incorporated and restructured it as a non-profit organization. The Pottery became one of the initial members of the Glen Echo Park Partnership for Arts and Culture (GEPPAC). Location: Glen Echo Pottery

events.description: Join a ranger for a 30-minute, family-friendly walk through Battleground National Cemetery and discover the stories of the soldiers buried here. We will be giving out maps and info to each holiday market for your convenience. Don't miss out on some delicious hot cocoa while you listen to our amazing carolers!

events.title: Join Historic Annapolis for 1776: Yuletide in Revolutionary Annapolis
events.description: Celebrate the Holiday Season Through the Spirit of America 250 with Historic Annapolis! As America commemorates its 250th anniversary, step back to the holiday season of 1776 and experience Yuletide in Annapolis at the William Paca House & Garden and the Hogshead Trades Museum. Discover how early Americans celebrated the season through traditional music, engaging storytelling, and festive customs that brought families and communities together during the nation’s founding era. It’s a unique opportunity to experience the sights, sounds, and traditions of the season while reflecting on the history of our country’s beginnings. Your Yuletide admission includes access to both historic sites, and you may begin your journey at either location. Cost: $15 for General Admissions. $10 for HA Members, Volunteers, and Military. $5 for Children age between 3-17. Free for Children age under 3. Timed entries for Colonial Yuletide Celebration: 2 pm 2:30 pm 3 pm 3:30 pm 4 pm 4:30 pm (last tour of the day) Advance registration strongly recommended; walk-ups will be accommodated as space permits. William Paca House and Garden 186 Prince George Street Annapolis, MD 21401 Join us as Annapolis Living Historians bring the elegant Georgian mansion to life with spirited gossip and political buzz from the Revolutionary era. Enjoy a 30-minute guided tour through candlelit rooms adorned with luminaries, festive garlands, and colonial holiday charm. Visit Santa Claus in the charming Summer House nestled within the Paca Garden. 2 pm -5 pm Enjoy colonial music with the accomplished musicians and singers of Create your own holiday craft and enjoy seasonal refreshments. Note: Regular docent guided 60-minute house tours are available at 10:30 am and 11:30 am. Accessibility Considerations : Accessing the interior of the William Paca House requires ascending and descending several flights of stairs. Visitors with limited mobility can access the brick Paca Garden Terrace via the driveway of the Paca Hous

events.title: Juice
events.description: Juice is a Boston-born alternative rock band whose sound moves freely among guitar-driven rock, pop, hip-hop and R&B, with violin adding an unexpected edge. The group’s 2021 project, Boy Story, threads songs about growing up, self-image and complicated relationships into a larger coming-of-age arc. “Superimposed” leans into synth-pop and hip-hop alongside its rock foundation, while “Girlfriend Song” brings a lively, wry take on identity and romance. That mix of catchy momentum and candid storytelling gives Juice’s songs room to shift in mood without losing their sense of drive.

Watch as over 10,000 twinkling holiday lights illuminate the vineyard vines, offering a spectacular view to kick off the night! Four-Course Wine Dinner After the lighting, walk the red carpet into the whimsically decorated stable for a sumptuous four-course dinner, expertly paired with Bluemont Vineyard wines. Each dish will showcase local ingredients sourced from Great Country Farms and other local purveyors, highlighting the finest flavors of the season. Wine & Vineyard Stories Throughout the evening, our team will share the rich history of Bluemont Vineyard and the stories behind each wine vintage, taking you on a journey from grape to glass. Holiday Toast End the night with a joyful toast to the holiday season, celebrating great friends, fine wine, and warm memories.

events.description: Once known as the Bowie-Johnson House, Linville Manor in Upper Marlboro was built in 1854 on the foundations of an earlier plantation home that burned mysteriously. The Overnight VIP package for two includes extended investigation time and a night in one of four haunted suites. Ages 18 and over, or 16-17 with a responsible adult. Tickets are limited.

events.description: Don’t miss our signature holiday event on Saturday, December 5! The event combines the magic of the holidays with recognition of the Marshall Plan countries. About the ERP The European Recovery Program (ERP) was a U.S. program that supplied nearly $13 billion to help finance rebuilding efforts in Europe in the wake of World War II. This program became known as the Marshall Plan because of George Marshall’s role in recognizing its importance and persuading Congress and the American people of its importance. Nearly 75 years later, the 17 nations that participated in the program continue to enjoy the peace and prosperity it helped secure for them.

events.title: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power
events.description: Necessary Means: Adreinne Waheed on Gathering and Power, an exhibition examining the beauty, dynamism, and political force of collective Black life across the African Diaspora through the photography of Howard alumna Adreinne Waheed. Curated by Kathryn Coney-Ali, executive director of the Howard University Gallery of Art, and Dr. Melanee C. Harvey-Fryar, associate professor of art history in the Chadwick A. Boseman College of Fine Arts, the exhibition brings Waheed’s documentary street photography into conversation with selections from the Waheed Photo Archive. Together, the works explore Black joy, protest, community, cultural tradition, and the power created when people gather. Necessary Means opens Wednesday, October 14, 2026, at the Howard University Museum in Founders Library and remains on view through May 28, 2027.

events.title: Nekisha Durrett & Virginia Shore in Conversation
events.description: Registration includes Museum admission. After the conversation, please join us for a glass of wine. Please note: parking onsite is limited and the use of ridesharing is encouraged. About Nekisha Durrett Nekisha Durrett is a Washington, DC-based artist whose work brings hidden and overlooked histories into public view. Grounded in deep research and material exploration, her multidisciplinary practice spans public art, installation, sculpture, painting, and social practice. Durrett is especially drawn to stories of Black life, labor, and imagination that have been forgotten or intentionally erased, creating spaces that hold both remembrance and possibility. Her work often begins with fragments—an archival image, a personal story, a neglected site—and evolves into layered forms that invite reflection, ritual, and collective memory. Through site-specific installations and collaborative processes, Durrett makes room for voices long silenced and for futures not yet written. Durrett’s permanent public artworks are found at Arlington Arts in Virginia, the Baltimore Museum of Art, Miami Dade County, the Phillips Collection and MLK Jr. Memorial Library in Washington, DC, the City of West Palm Beach, and Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania. Recent projects include Break Water in Alexandria, Don’t Forget to Remember (Me) at Bryn Mawr, and Queen City in Arlington. She recently concluded a fellowship with For Freedoms and Civics Arts Lab at the Corcoran and National Gallery of Art. In 2025, she was a Smithsonian Artist Research Fellow at the National Museum of African American History and Culture. Durrett’s large-scale, community-driven commission Hem of Heaven was unveiled at the Obama Presidential Center in June 2026. She holds a BFA from The Cooper Union and an MFA from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art and Design. events.description: Rooted in the sounds of Spanish Harlem, the Spanish Harlem Orchestra brings New York-style salsa dura and Latin jazz to life with a 13-piece ensemble of musicians and vocalists led by pianist and arranger Oscar Hernández. Its precise, full-bodied sound honors salsa’s rich history while making room for fresh arrangements and jazz improvisation. The group’s Grammy-winning albums include Across 110th Street, Viva La Tradición and Anniversary; its 2024 release, Swing Forever, features vocalist Gilberto Santa Rosa. events.title: The Mainliners
events.description: Raised in Southern California by parents who brought them to DIY punk shows and spun classic punk records in the house, Hollywood, CA-based punk up-and-comers, The Mainliners, are the real thing. And they embrace their roots, taking inspiration from such legendary SoCal bands as TSOL, Descendants, and DI, and drawing comparisons to others in the vanguard, from The Circle Jerks to The Adolescents. Formed in the crucible of pent-up creative energy that was a quarantine-era art/punk house in Los Angeles, the band hit the ground running - writing songs, playing shows, and switching instruments for a year and a half before the official four man lineup of Cash Mathieu on vocals, Colin Martin on guitar, Adrian Morris on bass, and Jackson Fox on drums was cemented. Since then, the band has been hard at work developing their musical and visual language across several singles, an EP, an album, and a live album, all released since 2023. They’ve been tearing up stages across the country and getting their name out there playing with bands such as Enjoy, Gvllow, Civic and Bad Nerves. They also played to a huge crowd as the only punk band on the 2024 edition of Tyler, The Creator’s Camp Flog Gnaw

Watch a blacksmith at work! Enjoy hot apple cider and heirloom-recipe baked goods. Children can make a craft and enjoy a visit with Belsnickel. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, Christmas in Catoctin Furnace included a visit from Belsnickel to the homes of German immigrants. events.title: Unfossilizing African Art
events.description: Presented after extensive research, this exhibition recontextualizes African material culture objects held in the GW Collection for nearly 50 years. Led by Assistant Professor Clement Akpang, 59 students from four seminar courses offered between Fall 2024 and Spring 2026, conducted original research to deepen understanding of the university’s holdings and update how we interpret and exhibit these objects. The exhibition features 37 tangible heritage objects, ranging from an Egúngún Paaka from Yorubaland to a Kii [brass pipe], attributed to the Baumum people of Cameroon, accompanied by images and video that illuminate their rich histories. Research on the entire collection is presented in an accompanying illustrated publication. Image: Once Known Mende carver [Mende, Sierra Leone], Sowei, 19th-20th century, wood, varnish, 16 H x 10 W x 10 D in. Gift of Stephen A. Spear, 1975 (P.75.2.30)

events.title: Wild On Your Door Holiday Wreath Workshop at Dirt Farm
events.description: Join us for a seasonal design session at Dirt Farm Brewing where you will create your very own holiday wreath with Walking Wind Farm and Florist! Step back into a time when holiday décor was gathered from the woods and the winter garden. Join us for an immersive workshop dedicated to the art of the traditional, textured wreath. Moving away from the commercial look of the modern holiday, we will focus on the rich diversity of "The Winter Field" - utilizing layered evergreens, architectural dried elements, and the "saved" treasures of late autumn. What You’ll Explore: The Power of Texture: Learn to layer multiple varieties of cedar, pine, and fir for a lush, professional-grade base. The Dried Garden: Integrating natural elements like seed pods, dried citrus, red chilis and flowers for a modern take on the "Nature-First" aesthetic. Organic Mechanics: Mastering the traditional wire-wrap technique to ensure your wreath stays fresh and secure through the season. Historical Design: How to create a balanced, asymmetrical, or classic circular design that honors the natural movement of the branches. Details: Date: Saturday, December 5 Time: 11:30-1:30pm OR 2-4pm Location: Dirt Farm Brewing, Bluemont, Va Investment: $75 - Includes a premium grapevine or wire base, a massive selection of textural greenery, and all specialty dried elements. events.description: Go beyond King Street on a 90-minute guided walk through Alexandria's remarkable Wilkes Street Cemetery Complex—13 historic cemeteries, 52 acres, and more than 35,000 burials in one walkable landscape.Led by independent historian and cemetery superintendent David Heiby, creator of Gravestone Stories, the tour connects Alexandria's past to the American Revolution, War of 1812, Civil War, Cold War, and more. Meet George Washington's pallbearers, Revolutionary War patriots, Civil War soldiers, a Soviet spy, and others whose stories illuminate more than two centuries of Alexandria history. Every stop is grounded in original research, cemetery records, and discoveries made within the complex, including graves rediscovered after nearly 200 years. Tours are limited to small groups. The 90-minute walk covers approximately 1 to 1.5 miles over historic cemetery paths and uneven terrain. Free parking is available.Tours are offered Fridays and Saturdays at 1:00 p.m., with an additional Thursday tour at 3:30 p.m. Tickets are $30 per person and include the official Gravestone Stories companion e-book. See the Gravestone Stories website for current availability and booking.

events.description: The Milkhouse Ford trail offers both beautifully forested nature and a glimpse into Washington DC’s history. Ramble with a ranger for a guided hike on this 1.7-mile loop, where you will encounter 5000 years of history, from traces of Indigenous land usage, to Fort DeRussy (which saw action during the Civil War), to the two-room log cabin used by poet Joaquin Miller, and to the historic Milkhouse Ford river crossing (one of Rock Creek Park’s oldest and most well-preserved fords). Meet at the Rock Creek Park Nature Center, bring plenty of water, dress for the weather, and be prepared for a fun and enjoyable outing.

events.description: The Blackbyrds performing this special concert on Thanksgiving weekend to celebrate 50 years since the release of “Rock Creek Park”, a classic song that has endured for generations! The band is one of the most successful ever from the DC area and came together in the 1970s as Howard University students under the guidance of their music professor, the late great jazz trumpeter Donald Byrd who became their manager and producer. They created a unique jazz funk sound combined with soulful harmonies that made a big impact on the music charts. The Blackbyrds’ biggest hit songs were “Walking In Rhythm”, their Grammy nominated million selling smash hit on both the R&B and pop charts; “Happy Music”, an uplifting party anthem that was their biggest R&B hit; and “Rock Creek Park”, their beloved song known for its infectious groove and famous verse “doin’ it in the park, doin’ it after dark, oh yeah…Rock Creek Park!” The Blackbyrds tour around the world but always look forward to performing in the DC area where they are most appreciated. The band’s original core members as well as new members are all from the DC area led by drummer Keith Killgo. Their crowd pleasing performance features all of their most popular songs plus those by Donald Byrd including “Places And Spaces” and “(Fallin’ Like) Dominoes.” SATURDAY, NOV 28. 2026 Dinner & Doors 6:00pm Showtime 8:00pm

events.description: Go beyond King Street on a 90-minute guided walk through Alexandria's remarkable Wilkes Street Cemetery Complex—13 historic cemeteries, 52 acres, and more than 35,000 burials in one walkable landscape. Led by independent historian and cemetery superintendent David Heiby, creator of Gravestone Stories, the tour connects Alexandria's past to the American Revolution, War of 1812, Civil War, Cold War, and more. Meet George Washington's pallbearers, Revolutionary War patriots, Civil War soldiers, a Soviet spy, and others whose stories illuminate more than two centuries of Alexandria history. Every stop is grounded in original research, cemetery records, and discoveries made within the complex, including graves rediscovered after nearly 200 years. Tours are limited to small groups. The 90-minute walk covers approximately 1 to 1.5 miles over historic cemetery paths and uneven terrain. Free parking is available. Tours are offered Fridays and Saturdays at 1:00 p.m., with an additional Thursday tour at 3:30 p.m. Tickets are $30 per person and include the official Gravestone Stories companion e-book. See the Gravestone Stories website for current availability and booking.

events.description: Go beyond King Street on a 90-minute guided walk through Alexandria's remarkable Wilkes Street Cemetery Complex—13 historic cemeteries, 52 acres, and more than 35,000 burials in one walkable landscape.Led by independent historian and cemetery superintendent David Heiby, creator of Gravestone Stories, the tour connects Alexandria's past to the American Revolution, War of 1812, Civil War, Cold War, and more. Meet George Washington's pallbearers, Revolutionary War patriots, Civil War soldiers, a Soviet spy, and others whose stories illuminate more than two centuries of Alexandria history. Every stop is grounded in original research, cemetery records, and discoveries made within the complex, including graves rediscovered after nearly 200 years. Tours are limited to small groups. The 90-minute walk covers approximately 1 to 1.5 miles over historic cemetery paths and uneven terrain. Free parking is available.Tours are offered Fridays and Saturdays at 1:00 p.m., with an additional Thursday tour at 3:30 p.m. Tickets are $30 per person and include the official Gravestone Stories companion e-book. See the Gravestone Stories website for current availability and booking.

events.description: This December, our community comes together to honor stories of courage that span generations. Join neighbors, volunteers, and park staff as we light the grounds of Battleground National Cemetery in a heartfelt tribute to those who served our nation. Each glowing lantern represents a life lost—41 US soldiers resting at Battleground National Cemetery and those who lost their lives on December 7, 1941, at Pearl Harbor. As we walk the illuminated path together, we’ll reflect on their legacy and the ways their sacrifices continue to shape our shared history. Everyone is welcome. Bring your family, your friends, and your heart. Let’s gather as a community to remember, reflect, and keep their light shining.
